stem: In a medical treatment study comparing Drug X vs. Drug Y: Overall, Treatment Y has a higher recovery rate (62.7% vs 61.4%). However, when stratified by disease severity: In mild cases (n_X=40, n_Y=80): Treatment X achieves 89% vs Treatment Y's 69%. In severe cases (n_X=100, n_Y=30): Treatment X achieves 50% vs Treatment Y's 45%. The true population proportion of mild cases is uncertain, estimated between 38% and 62%. Which treatment is actually better, and by how much? Report the adjusted difference in recovery rate (X - Y) as a proportion to three decimal places.

ground_truth.answer: This is Simpson's Paradox. Treatment X is better in BOTH subgroups. The aggregate reversal occurs because X is disproportionately applied to severe cases (harder cases). Adjusted difference (X - Y): [0.107, 0.143], point estimate: 0.125. Treatment X is genuinely better by 12.5 percentage points.

solution_steps: Aggregate rates: X=61.4%, Y=62.7% (Y appears better).
Stratified: In mild cases: X=89% > Y=69%. In severe cases: X=50% > Y=45%.
X is better in BOTH subgroups — this is Simpson's Paradox.
The paradox arises because Drug X is applied more to severe cases (lower baseline rate), skewing the aggregate.
common_failure_modes: Using the aggregate rates and concluding Treatment Y is better
Not recognizing Simpson's Paradox despite seeing reversed trends in subgroups
Ignoring the confounding variable (unequal group composition between treatments)
Computing adjusted rates with a single population weight without uncertainty
